title: THE BIBLE NAMES A WOMAN WHO GAVE BIRTH TO THREE SONS—BUT THE FATHER’S NAME IS MISSING FROM THE VERSE. WHY?
paragraphs: THE BIBLE NAMES A WOMAN WHO GAVE BIRTH TO THREE SONS—BUT THE FATHER’S NAME IS MISSING FROM THE VERSE. WHY?

Buried in a genealogy most Christians skip is a woman named Naarah, three sons whose names survived thousands of years, and a surprising reminder that being overlooked by people does not mean being forgotten by God.
There is something unsettling about seeing your name in a story while wondering whether anyone truly knows what you have lived through.
Some people know your family but not your pain.
They know your children but not the sacrifices you made raising them.
They know your last name but not the nights you cried behind closed doors.
And sometimes, the hardest part of your story is not what people have said about you.
It is what they never bothered to ask.
Now imagine opening your Bible and discovering a woman whose name has survived for thousands of years, along with the names of three sons she bore.
But when you read the verse, something seems to be missing.
The father is not named there.
And if you read too quickly, you might assume the Bible has left behind a family mystery.
But slow down.
Because the truth is more interesting than the mystery.
And what Scripture actually says may challenge the way we think about forgotten people, complicated family histories, and the God who sees what others overlook.
Her name was Naarah.
And her story appears in one of the most frequently skipped sections of the Bible.
First Chronicles.
Chapter four.
Verses five through seven.
The kind of passage where names seem to tumble across the page without explanation.
The kind of passage many believers hurry through because they are searching for something more immediately inspiring.
A promise.
A miracle.
A dramatic encounter.
A word from heaven.
But sometimes we are so busy looking for God in the extraordinary that we fail to recognize the significance of what He has preserved in the ordinary.
Listen carefully to the words of Scripture.
“And Ashur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah.” — 1 Chronicles 4:5, KJV
Then comes the verse that catches our attention.
“And Naarah bare him Ahuzam, and Hepher, and Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah.” — 1 Chronicles 4:6, KJV
Wait.
Did you catch that?
The popular description of this passage says a woman gave birth to three sons without the father being named in the same verse.
But that description needs an important correction.
The Bible actually names four sons of Naarah, not three.
Ahuzam.
Hepher.
Temeni.
Haahashtari.
And although Ashhur's name does not appear again in verse six, the father is not missing from the passage.
He has already been introduced in verse five.
Even more importantly, the original Hebrew of verse six explicitly connects the children to him.
The Hebrew begins:
וַתֵּלֶד לוֹ נַעֲרָה
Vattēled lô Naʿărāh.
Literally:
“And Naarah bore to him...”
Those two Hebrew words, vattēled lô, matter.
The verb vattēled means “and she bore” or “and she gave birth.”
The word lô means “to him” or “for him.”
The masculine pronoun points back to Ashhur, the man identified in the preceding verse.
So the biblical writer was not concealing a father.
He was continuing a family record already in progress.
There is no textual basis for claiming that Naarah's children were fatherless, illegitimate, abandoned, or born into a secret scandal.
Scripture simply does not say those things.
And we should never manufacture a scandal where God has not revealed one.
But there is still something worth noticing.
The chronicler does not merely identify these children as descendants of Ashhur.
He concludes by identifying them as the sons of Naarah.
Her name is repeated.
Her motherhood is remembered.
Her place in the family record is preserved.
And in a genealogy that largely follows fathers and sons, the presence of these women's names deserves our attention.
Not because we can prove that Naarah was rejected, wounded, or mistreated.
We cannot.
Not because we know she lived through a heartbreaking family crisis.
We do not.
But because her name reminds us that even passages filled with unfamiliar people belong to the larger story of God's dealings with His people.
And perhaps that is where this ancient record begins to touch something painfully familiar.
Because some of you know what it feels like to contribute to a story while someone else receives most of the recognition.
You carried responsibilities nobody applauded.
You gave your strength to people who rarely noticed how exhausted you were.
You worked.
You provided.
You prayed.
You forgave.
You kept showing up.
And somewhere along the way, you began to wonder whether the quiet parts of your life mattered at all.
The Bible does not tell us that Naarah felt any of these things.
But the question her brief appearance raises can still lead us to a much larger biblical truth.
Does God see the people the world barely notices?
The answer is yes.
And Scripture gives us a much fuller account of that truth in the life of another woman.
Hagar.
A servant whose suffering is recorded in Genesis 16.
When Hagar fled into the wilderness, the angel of the LORD encountered her.
She was not invisible to God.
And after that encounter, she gave Him a remarkable name.
“Thou God seest me.” — Genesis 16:13, KJV
In Hebrew, the expression is associated with:
אֵל רֳאִי
El Roʾi.
Often rendered “God who sees me” or “God of seeing.”
Think about that.
A woman in the wilderness.
Far from security.
Caught in circumstances larger than herself.
And the God of heaven saw her.
Not because she was famous.
Not because she had influence.
Not because her life looked impressive to the people around her.
He saw her because He is God.
And His knowledge of human lives is not limited by human attention.
Maybe you needed that reminder today.
Not because your story is identical to Hagar's.
Not because every hardship means God is secretly preparing public recognition.
But because the Lord's awareness of your life does not depend on how many people notice you.
You may be overlooked.
You are not beyond His sight.
You may be misunderstood.
You are not beyond His knowledge.
You may be carrying a burden that no one around you fully understands.
You are not beyond His compassion.
And that matters more than you realize.
Because one of the enemy's cruelest temptations is to persuade wounded people that their suffering proves they have been abandoned.
That if God truly cared, their lives would look different by now.
That if their prayers mattered, the answers would have come sooner.
That if they were valuable, somebody would have recognized their sacrifices.
But the Gospel does not measure your worth by recognition.
It points you to Jesus Christ.
And Jesus repeatedly showed compassion to people whom others were willing to pass by.
He spoke to the Samaritan woman at the well.
He welcomed children whom His disciples initially tried to turn away.
He touched lepers.
He called a despised tax collector to follow Him.
He noticed a poor widow giving two small coins.
And He showed mercy to a dying criminal who had nothing left to offer Him but a desperate appeal.
These encounters were not all the same.
Their circumstances were different.
Their sins, needs, and responses were different.
But together they reveal something beautiful about the Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to affirm the people who already looked important. He came to seek and save the lost.
Luke 19:10 declares:
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.”
That is where the deepest hope of this story begins.
Not in the suggestion that Naarah had a hidden scandal.
Not in speculation about her marriage.
Not in imagining a dramatic history that Scripture never records.
But in recognizing that the same Bible preserving ancient genealogies eventually brings us to the One in whom God's promises find their fulfillment.
Jesus Christ.
The One who entered human history.
The One who took on flesh.
The One who lived without sin.
The One who bore our sins on the cross.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One who offers forgiveness and reconciliation with God to those who repent and believe.
And here is something that should stop every reader in their tracks.
The opening chapter of Matthew also contains a genealogy.
A long record of generations leading to Jesus Christ.
And within that genealogy, several women are specifically mentioned.
Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
The wife of Uriah, whom we know from the Old Testament as Bathsheba.
And Mary, the mother of Jesus.
Their stories are not interchangeable.
Some involve suffering.
Some involve moral failure by others.
Some reveal remarkable faith.
Some unfold amid deeply complicated circumstances.
But Matthew's genealogy makes one thing unmistakable.
God's redemptive purpose was not defeated by the brokenness of human history.
And that does not mean God approves of sin.
He does not.
It means human sin and failure cannot overthrow His sovereign purposes.
This is where we must be careful.
Nor does it mean that grace erases the reality of wrongdoing.
Grace does something far greater.
It confronts our sin with truth.
It calls us to repentance.
It brings forgiveness through Christ.
It gives us a new standing before God.
And it begins transforming the way we live.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
Notice those words.
In Christ.
That is the center.
Not in self-improvement.
Not in religious performance.
Not in the applause of people.
Not in pretending your past never happened.
In Christ.
And perhaps this is the part of the article that becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is possible to spend years asking God to heal the wounds other people caused while refusing to confront the sins we ourselves have committed.
We want comfort.
But not correction.
We want restoration.
But not repentance.
We want peace.
But we keep protecting the very habits that are destroying our peace.
We want Jesus to rewrite our story.
But we resist surrendering the pen.
And the Gospel lovingly refuses to leave us there.
Jesus did not die simply to make us feel better about remaining unchanged.
He died to save sinners.
He rose again so that those who belong to Him might walk in newness of life.
His grace is not permission to continue comfortably in rebellion.
It is the undeserved mercy that brings us back to God and teaches us to live differently.
So perhaps the most important question today is not whether anyone knows your story.
Perhaps it is whether you have truly surrendered that story to Christ.
The shame.
The resentment.
The secret compromises.
The bitterness you keep justifying.
The guilt you bury beneath religious activity.
The fear that God could never forgive what you have done.
You do not need to invent a cleaner past before coming to Jesus.
You need to come to Him in truth.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust His finished work.
And receive the mercy that no amount of human approval could ever purchase.
First John 1:9 gives believers this assurance:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Read that again.
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because the blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient.
And maybe, for the first time in a long time, you need to stop performing strength and admit that your soul is tired.
You have been telling people you are fine.
You have been smiling through spiritual exhaustion.
You have been attending church while quietly struggling to pray.
You know the right Christian words.
But behind those words, there are battles you have not told anyone about.
If that is you, do not mistake your exhaustion for the end of your story.
Come to Christ.
Seek the help and encouragement of faithful believers.
Open the Scriptures again.
Pray, even if the words come slowly.
And remember that God's faithfulness is not measured by the intensity of your emotions.
Not as a performance.
Not because writing those words earns forgiveness.
But as a simple, honest expression of your desire to keep walking with Jesus.
There is something powerful about a community of believers that does more than admire spiritual words.
A community that actually prays.
That opens the Bible.
That speaks truth with compassion.
That helps one another persevere.
And this is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to turn biblical mysteries into sensational stories.
Not to make promises God never made.
Not to build faith on emotional excitement alone.
But to bring people back to the living Word of God and to the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
Because the world is already overflowing with noise.
What we desperately need is truth.
Truth that corrects us when we are wrong.
Truth that comforts us when we are weary.
Truth that exposes sin without hiding the mercy of the Savior.
Truth that does not collapse when the emotional moment has passed.
Every time you share a Scripture-centered article, you help place biblical encouragement in front of someone who may never have searched for it themselves.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be carrying grief you know nothing about.
Someone may be quietly wrestling with faith.
Someone may have walked away from church.
Someone may believe their past has placed them beyond forgiveness.
And one article, faithfully pointing them to Christ, may become an invitation to open their Bible again.
Not to pressure your friends.
Not to prove your devotion.
But because the Gospel is worth sharing.
There is room here for honest questions.
For biblical learning.
For repentance.
For encouragement.
For growing deeper in Christ.
It is a practical partnership in continuing and expanding this Scripture-centered ministry.
But it is important to say this clearly.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
But they can serve as everyday reminders of biblical truth, meaningful gifts, and practical tools for encouragement and discipleship.
These resources are there to help believers grow deeper in Jesus Christ, study the Scriptures, develop a more consistent devotional life, and become spiritually equipped to encourage others.
Because biblical nourishment should never be presented as something that only paying supporters deserve.
If that is a mission you believe in, and you are able to support it, you are warmly invited to join us.
But before you leave, return with me to that ancient genealogy.
First Chronicles 4.
A man named Ashhur.
Two wives named Helah and Naarah.
Four sons of Naarah.
And then another verse.
“And the sons of Helah were, Zereth, and Jezoar, and Ethnan.” — 1 Chronicles 4:7, KJV
There they are.
The three sons.
But they belong to Helah, not Naarah.
And even in that verse, the father's name is understood from the family context established earlier.
That is the important distinction.
Naarah is associated with four sons in verse six.
Helah is associated with three sons in verse seven.
Ashhur is identified in verse five.
A seemingly mysterious passage becomes clearer when we stop isolating a single sentence and begin reading Scripture in context.
And perhaps there is a lesson in that too.
How often do we judge a person's life from one isolated moment?
One mistake.
One photograph.
One rumor.
One chapter.
One painful season.
We see a fragment and assume we know the whole story.
But we do not.
And while this genealogy does not teach us that Naarah was a victim of misunderstanding, it can remind us how easily misunderstanding arises when we read incompletely.
That is why context matters.
In Scripture.
In relationships.
In the way we speak about others.
And especially in the way we understand the Gospel.
Because if you only look at the cross without understanding sin, you may miss why Jesus died.
If you only look at sin without understanding grace, you may despair.
If you only look at grace without repentance, you may misunderstand what salvation changes.
And if you only look at your past without looking to the risen Christ, you may begin believing that the worst thing you ever did has the final word over your life.
It does not have to.
Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
Forgiveness is real.
Repentance is possible.
New life is available in Him.
The record of Naarah does not tell us how her life ended, what she feared, or what she hoped for.
We should be humble enough to leave those unanswered questions where Scripture leaves them.
But the Bible does tell us enough about Jesus to answer the question that matters eternally.
Can a sinner truly be forgiven?
Yes.
Can someone enslaved to sin be changed?
Yes, through the saving and transforming grace of God.
Can someone whose life has been marked by shame find a new identity?
Yes, in Christ.
Not because the past was imaginary.
Not because consequences always disappear.
But because Jesus is greater than the sin and shame that once ruled us.
And if there is one thing I hope you carry away from these ancient names, let it be this:
Do not build your faith on the mysteries Scripture leaves unexplained when God has already revealed the Savior you desperately need.
Was it discovering that Naarah actually had four sons named in the text?
Was it realizing that Ashhur was already identified as the father?
Or was it the reminder that your hope is not in being remembered by the world, but in belonging to Jesus Christ?
Your response may encourage someone else to open their Bible and read more carefully.
Because somewhere tonight, a person is sitting alone, convinced that their story is already ruined.
They think their failures have spoken too loudly.
Their shame has lasted too long.
Their mistakes have gone too far.
And they cannot imagine that anything beautiful could come after what has happened.
Maybe that person is someone you know.
Maybe that person is you.
If so, hear the Gospel one more time.
The cross is not evidence that your sin was small.
It is evidence that sin was so serious that the Son of God gave His life to save sinners.
And the empty tomb declares that death did not have the final word.
So come to Jesus.
Not with a polished version of yourself.
Not with excuses.
Not with a promise that you will somehow save yourself.
Come in repentance and faith.
Come to the One who died and rose again.
Come to the Savior who receives those who turn to Him.
Your past may explain where you have been, but it does not have to decide who you become when your life is surrendered to Christ.
